title: A yearly pilgrimage
hookLine: to a temple, a tree, a mountain
tomorrow: friends are the whole path. so why a poem about walking alone?

lines: A TEACHER OF LETTING GO, GIVING DIRECTIONS.
cards: People cross oceans to stand in a stadium where a band once played, or outside the house where a grandmother raised them. Ông, Mai's grandfather, wants her to visit the temple he walked into when he first came to this country.
It's across town from her summer program. Here's the strange part: the Buddha sent people on trips like that too. In the long sutta of his last days, Ananda is worried.

While the Buddha lives, monks come from everywhere to see him. After he's gone, who will they come to see? And the teacher who spent his life saying everything passes, don't cling, answers by giving directions.

teach.h: FOUR PLACES, NAMED BEFORE HE DIED.
teach.b: He names four places. Where the Tathagata was born. Where he woke up.
Where he first set the wheel of the teaching turning. Where he passed away. A person of faith, he says, should go and see them.
So why would a teacher of letting go point at ground?
Look at how the sutta describes them: places that stir samvega, a jolt of awe and urgency. Not places that hand out blessings. Places that wake you up.
At the birthplace you remember he was a child once, like anyone. Where he awoke, that it can be done. Where he first taught, that it was meant to be shared.
Where he died, that even he died.

teach.h: EACH ONE POINTS BACK AT THE TEACHING.
teach.b: Every one of them points back at the teaching, not at the dirt.
That's why Buddhists still travel to Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar, the places tradition matches to those four, walking around the shrines and leaving flowers.

teach.h: A TEMPLE, A TREE, A MOUNTAIN.
teach.b: And it's why a smaller trip counts too: a temple, a tree, a mountain, a temple across town where a young man, new to a country, first found his footing.
The ground doesn't do the work. It reminds you to.

how: Buddhists from many countries travel to the places tradition links to the Buddha's birth, awakening, first teaching and passing (Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar), and also make smaller trips to temples, stupas, sacred trees and mountains, walking around shrines and offering flowers.

o: a yearly fee paid to a temple to keep its blessings
a vow to walk barefoot to every well-known temple once
a trip made on purpose to a place that stirs your practice

games.q: inside the four places — tap the pairs.
p: worried no one would come once he was gone
a jolt of awe and urgency
reminds you; it doesn't do the work

s: a holy place gives a blessing to anyone who stands on it
the sutta describes the four places as stirring samvega, awe and urgency, that points you back to the teaching.
the Buddha himself named places worth visiting after his death
when Ananda worried, he named four: his birth, awakening, first teaching and passing.
a pilgrimage only counts if it's long and far from home
the four places are the well-known ones, but a temple, a tree or a mountain across town can stir the same thing.

games.q: your cousin is saving up for a trip to Bodh Gaya and asks what she should be there for. what fits the sutta best?
o: to remember what happened there and let it stir her own practice
to collect a blessing she couldn't get anywhere else at home
mostly the sights; the deeper meaning of the place is for monks
games.why: the Buddha named the places so people would be stirred to remember: it can be done, it was shared, even he died. they point back at the teaching.

practice: Pick one place you could go on purpose this year: a temple, a tree, a hill, a grave, a kitchen where someone taught you something.
Ask yourself what you want it to remind you of, what usually gets in the way, and one plan to get there, a date, a ride, who comes along. Then rest with that place in mind while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: A yearly pilgrimage: a trip made on purpose, to a place that wakes up what you already know.

orig.note: Pali: a jolt of awe and urgency; the four places are described as stirring it.

carryVoice: Your line: a place to go. The ground reminds you, and you do the walking. That's thirteen days into the block.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta) 5.8 (the four places that stir samvega)
